newsitem.title: UK: Zaire rebel advance causes spike in cobalt prices.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel advance causes spike in cobalt prices.

text.p: Cobalt prices rose on Monday on news that major producer Gecamines closed its headquarters in Lubumbashi as Zaire rebels advanced on the city.
Despite the start of peace talks in South Africa rebels continued an advance into Zaire's mineral rich region of Shaba.
Gecamines closed its headquarters as forces of Laurent Kabila took the town of Kipushi which is around 30 km away.
In London Gecamines were unavailable for comment, though one source close to the producer of cobalt and copper said there had been little metal flowing from Zaire recently.
One trader believed that Gecamines have made no plans for medium and long-term contracts.
"Production is at a standstill and is likely to remain so," the trader said.
But traders added that nobody who had secured effective political control of Shaba would want to shut in production of a hard currency earner like cobalt for very long.
Zaire has recently been producing around 5,000 tonnes of cobalt and 40,000 tonnes of copper a year.
The copper is marginal to world supply but the cobalt forms roughly one fifth of global output of all grades of that metal.
Cobalt is used in the aerospace and battery industries. World stocks have been declining but new production and extra volume from upgraded mines is coming on stream.
European traders and merchants marked high grade cobalt up to around $25 a pound, while the lower graded Russian metal was quoted near $22.00.
In the early part of 1997 high grade material had eased to around $19.
The conflict in Zaire was having no impact on the European copper market. The recent annual production from Zaire of around 40,000 tonnes compares with some 500,000 in the early 1980s.
